matching.reasoningTemplate: Palpitations ± breathlessness suggest a tachyarrhythmia; an ECG is the key test.

clinicalPearls: AF is the most common sustained arrhythmia; prevalence rises steeply with age (~20% of those over 80), and the lifetime risk for a 40-year-old man is roughly one in four (p.1990).
On the ECG, AF shows absence of organized atrial activity (no P waves) with an irregularly irregular ventricular response; the chaotic atrial activity is often best seen in lead V1 (p.1990, 1991).

The conducted ventricular rate is variable and usually rapid (commonly 110-160/min), but may exceed 200/min, or be inappropriately slow when there is high vagal tone or AV nodal conduction disease (p.1990).
Many patients are unaware of the irregular heartbeat, so AF is frequently asymptomatic; absence of AF on intermittent monitoring does not establish low risk (p.1990, 1993).

AF is categorized by temporal pattern: paroxysmal (self-terminating, usually within 7 days), persistent (continuous >7 days but <1 year), and long-standing persistent (>1 year); these patterns correlate with progressive left atrial enlargement and scar burden (p.1990, 1991).

Stroke and bleeding risks are estimated as concepts using the CHA2DS2-VASc score (stroke risk: congestive heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA, vascular disease, sex) and HAS-BLED score (bleeding risk), respectively (p.1993).

AF burden does not predict stroke risk; the approach to paroxysmal AF is the same as for persistent AF, and even apparently infrequent episodes carry risk because asymptomatic episodes are common (p.1993).
Subclinical AF detectable only on long-term continuous monitoring is associated with roughly 2.5-fold increased stroke risk (p.1993).
AF detected after cryptogenic stroke using insertable cardiac monitors in up to ~8.9% of patients within 6 months, supporting prolonged rhythm monitoring in this setting (p.1990).
harrison.pathophysiology: AF is characterized by disorganized, rapid, irregular atrial electrical activation with loss of organized atrial mechanical contraction; the AV node filters these impulses to produce an irregular ventricular rate. The pathophysiology is multifactorial and incompletely understood, with a proposed 'final common pathway' in which risk factors (age, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, alcohol, sleep-disordered breathing) drive electrophysiologic changes in atrial tissue. Altered membrane channel regulation produces abnormal excitability; pulmonary vein musculature (and other foci such as the posterior left atrial wall, superior vena cava, coronary sinus, vein of Marshall) shows enhanced automaticity generating ectopic beats that initiate AF. Progressive cellular and tissue remodeling shortens atrial refractory periods and creates functional reentry, with eventual fibrosis and left atrial enlargement, explaining the typical progression from paroxysmal to persistent to long-standing persistent disease. Loss of atrial systole reduces cardiac output, and variable ventricular filling produces variable stroke volume (p.1990-1992).
additionalDifferentials: Multifocal atrial tachycardia (>=3 distinct P-wave morphologies with clear isoelectric intervals and a slower atrial rate than AF; typically in chronic pulmonary disease and acute illness) (p.1989).

Other supraventricular tachycardias including atrial flutter, focal atrial tachycardia, AV nodal reentry, and AV reciprocating tachycardia, distinguished by 12-lead ECG appearance and response to AV nodal blockade (p.1976-1977).
Preexcited (accessory-pathway) AF, presenting as an irregular wide-complex tachycardia with bizarre, beat-to-beat-variable QRS morphology (p.1985-1986).
additionalInvestigations: Transesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion when AF duration is >48 h or unknown (p.1992).
Cardiac CT angiography with delayed-acquisition imaging as an alternative to TEE for left atrial appendage thrombus detection, with high sensitivity and specificity (p.1992).
Ambulatory ECG monitoring, implantable loop recorders, or wearable/home ECG devices to capture intermittent or subclinical episodes (p.1991, 1993).
redFlags: Acute AF with significant haemodynamic compromise, pulmonary oedema, or evidence of coronary ischaemia indicates need for emergent cardioversion (p.1992).

Preexcited AF over an accessory pathway with very rapid repetitive conduction (minimum R-R <250 ms occurs in ~25% of preexciting pathways) is potentially life-threatening, predisposing to ventricular fibrillation and sudden death (p.1985-1986).
Syncope or presyncope from bradycardia/pauses, including offset pauses on spontaneous conversion to sinus rhythm, suggesting coexisting sinus node dysfunction (tachy-brady syndrome) (p.1992).
Sustained uncontrolled rapid ventricular rates risk precipitating heart failure and tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (p.1990, 1992).
harrison.prognosis: AF is not benign: it carries a 1.5- to 1.9-fold increased mortality after adjusting for underlying cardiac disease, and causes approximately 25% of all strokes. It increases the risk of dementia, MRI-detected silent embolic infarcts, congestive heart failure, and cardiomyopathy. Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is generally reversible once ventricular rate is controlled. AF tends to be progressive, with no definitive durable cure, and patients maintaining sinus rhythm generally have better survival than those who remain in AF (p.1990, 1992, 1994).
pitfalls: Relying on AF burden or symptom frequency to gauge stroke risk is mistaken; anticoagulation decisions should rest on the risk-factor profile, not how often AF is documented (p.1993).
A normal intermittent monitor does not exclude clinically important AF, since asymptomatic episodes are common (p.1993).

Cardioverting AF of >48 h (or unknown) duration without anticoagulation or thrombus exclusion risks thromboembolism, which can occur even days later because of post-conversion atrial stunning (delayed recovery of mechanical function) (p.1992).
Nonvalvular AF (AF without mitral stenosis) differs in management from valvular AF; rheumatic mitral stenosis and mechanical valves carry especially high thromboembolic risk (p.1993).
harrison.severityClassification: By temporal pattern: paroxysmal AF (self-terminates or is cardioverted within 7 days; normal-to-mildly enlarged left atrium, low scar burden), persistent AF (continuous >7 days but <1 year; mild-to-severe LA enlargement, moderate scar), and long-standing persistent AF (>1 year; severely enlarged LA, high scar burden). A newer staged framework (at risk of AF, pre-AF, AF, permanent AF) reframes AF as a disease continuum. Mitral stenosis defines valvular versus nonvalvular AF for risk purposes (p.1991, 1993, 1996).
